Comfortedst
KUM-fer-ted-st
v.
From Old French conforter (to strengthen greatly), from Latin confortare; the archaic second-person singular past tense ("thou comfortedst") appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Isaiah's short psalm of thanksgiving.

Biblical Definition

Though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me.

Comfortedst appears once in the Authorized Version, in Isaiah 12, a brief psalm of praise placed immediately after the great oracles of judgment and the promised virgin-born child of Isaiah 7-11, functioning as the fitting response once salvation has come: O LORD, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me. The verse holds both realities together without softening either: real divine anger, justly provoked, and real divine comfort, freely given once that anger is turned away — not by pretending the anger was never deserved, but by the LORD Himself accomplishing the turning. The psalm continues in words later echoed throughout redemptive history: behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation (Isa 12:2), language the New Testament applies directly to the joy of gospel salvation, drawing water out of the wells of salvation (Isa 12:3) becoming an image used at the Feast of Tabernacles and taken up by Christ Himself when he stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink (Joh 7:37-38).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from COMFORT: to strengthen the mind under affliction; the archaic second-person singular past tense here of God turning away His anger and comforting the repentant.

expand to see more

COMFORT, v.t. To strengthen the mind under affliction; to console; to give solace.

COMFORTEDST, v. Archaic second-person singular past tense: thou didst comfort.

In Isaiah 12:1 the word marks the turning of God's just anger into comfort and salvation.

The short psalm follows the promised child of Isaiah 7-11, the fitting response to salvation accomplished.

Isaiah 12:3, 'draw water out of the wells of salvation,' is applied by Christ in John 7:37-38.

Key Scripture

Isa 12:1 — "And in that day thou shalt say, O LORD, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me."

Modern Corruption

A therapeutic reading that wants comfort without any real acknowledgment of God's just anger against sin misses that Isaiah's psalm holds both together, comfort arriving precisely because the LORD Himself turned away a wrath that was genuinely deserved.

expand to see more

A theology built only on divine comfort, without divine anger against sin first justly provoked, cannot account for what this psalm actually says; the comfort is meaningful precisely because the anger was real and the turning was God's own gracious act, not a denial that anger was ever warranted.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the psalm's own sequence: wrath justly kindled, wrath graciously turned, comfort freely given, and praise the only fitting response, a pattern fulfilled in the gospel Christ Himself invoked at the Feast of Tabernacles (Joh 7:37-38).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Comfortedst occurs once, in Isaiah's short psalm of praise following the promised child of Isaiah 7-11, holding together God's just anger, turned away, and the comfort that follows, language later applied by Christ to gospel salvation.

Comfortedst in Isaiah 12:1 marks the turning of God's just anger into comfort.

The psalm follows immediately after the promised virgin-born child of Isaiah 7-11.

Isaiah 12:2 continues: 'the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation.'

Isaiah 12:3 pictures salvation as wells of water to be drawn with joy.

Christ applies this image directly in John 7:37-38: 'If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.'

Usage

"Though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me."

"Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid (Isa 12:2)."

"If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink (Joh 7:37) — Christ's own application of this psalm's image."
